Box Plots with ggplot2

R
ggplot2
Data Visualization
Tutorial
A step-by-step guide to evolving a basic box plot into an advanced, publication-ready visualization
Author

Joao Luiz D’Andrea

Published

October 14, 2025

Introduction

In this tutorial, we’ll explore how to create increasingly sophisticated box plots using ggplot2. We’ll start with a basic plot and progressively add elements to make it more informative and visually appealing.

Box plots are excellent for comparing distributions across categories, showing median, quartiles, and outliers in a compact format.

We’ll use the built-in mtcars dataset from R, which contains specifications and performance data for 32 automobiles from 1973-74.

Setup

First, let’s load the required packages and prepare our data:

# Load required libraries
library(tidyverse)  # Includes ggplot2, dplyr, and other essential packages
library(scales)     # For formatting axes and labels

# Prepare the data: convert cylinders to factor and add car names
data_cars <- mtcars %>%
  mutate(
    cyl = factor(cyl, levels = c(4, 6, 8)),       # Convert to ordered factor
    car_name = rownames(mtcars)                    # Add car names as column
  )

# Preview the data
head(data_cars)

Chart 1: Basic Box Plot

Let’s start with a simple box plot showing fuel efficiency (miles per gallon) by number of cylinders.

ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg)) +  # Set up the plot with x and y variables
  geom_boxplot()                             # Create box plot

Code Explanation

Line 1: ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg)) - Initializes the plot with our car data, mapping cylinder count to the x-axis and miles per gallon to the y-axis

Line 2: geom_boxplot() - Adds box plots showing the five-number summary (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum) and outliers for each cylinder group

What we have so far: A functional but basic box plot. The statistical summaries are visible but the chart lacks context, visual appeal, and proper formatting.

Chart 2: Intermediate Enhancement

Now we’ll improve the chart by adding color, notches for confidence intervals, better labels, and applying a clean theme.

What we’re adding in this evolution:

  • Color fill to distinguish each cylinder group
  • Notched boxes showing confidence intervals around medians
  • Improved axis labels and title for clarity
  • Clean theme to remove visual clutter
  • Professional color palette from ColorBrewer
  • Individual data points overlaid for transparency
ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl)) +      # Add fill aesthetic
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.7) +                  # Notched boxes with transparency
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) +          # Add jittered points
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +                      # Apply color palette
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Decreases with More Cylinders",  # Main title
    subtitle = "Miles per gallon distribution for 32 automobiles (1973-74)",  # Subtitle
    x = "Number of Cylinders",                                # X-axis label
    y = "Miles Per Gallon"                                    # Y-axis label
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +                                           # Clean, minimal theme
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14),     # Bold title
    legend.position = "none"                                  # Remove redundant legend
  )

Code Explanation

Line 1: aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl) - Maps cylinder count to both x-axis position and fill color for visual distinction

Line 2: geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.7) - Creates box plots with notches (showing 95% confidence intervals around medians) and 70% opacity

Line 3: geom_jitter(width = 0.2, alpha = 0.4, size = 2) - Adds individual data points with controlled horizontal spread to show the actual sample distribution

Line 4: scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") - Applies a professional, colorblind-friendly palette from ColorBrewer

Lines 5-10: labs() - Adds descriptive title, subtitle, and axis labels to provide context

Line 11: theme_minimal() - Applies a clean theme with minimal visual elements

Lines 12-15: theme() - Customizes title formatting and removes the legend since cylinder count is already shown on x-axis

What we have now: A much more informative chart with color differentiation, confidence intervals via notches, and transparency showing all data points. The clean theme and proper labeling make it presentation-ready.

Chart 3: Advanced Visualization

Let’s take it to the next level with custom styling, statistical annotations, summary statistics, and polished formatting suitable for publication.

What we’re adding in this final evolution:

  • Custom color palette optimized for accessibility
  • Mean markers shown as diamonds overlaid on boxes
  • Sample size annotations showing number of cars in each category
  • Statistical comparison lines indicating significant differences
  • Enhanced typography with refined spacing
  • Outlier highlighting with custom styling
  • Data source caption for proper attribution
  • Refined spacing and margins for professional appearance
# Calculate summary statistics for annotations
cyl_summary <- data_cars %>%
  group_by(cyl) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),                                       # Count per category
    median_mpg = median(mpg),                      # Median mpg
    mean_mpg = mean(mpg),                          # Mean mpg
    .groups = 'drop'
  )

# Define custom color palette (colorblind-friendly)
cyl_colors <- c(
  "4" = "#52A675",                                 # Green for best efficiency
  "6" = "#F4A261",                                 # Orange for medium
  "8" = "#E76F51"                                  # Red for lowest efficiency
)

ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = cyl)) +
  # Box plot layer with custom styling
  geom_boxplot(notch = TRUE, alpha = 0.6,
               outlier.shape = 21,                 # Hollow circles for outliers
               outlier.size = 3,
               outlier.fill = "white",
               outlier.color = "gray30",
               color = "gray30",
               linewidth = 0.6) +
  # Add jittered data points
  geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.3, 
              size = 2, color = "gray20") +
  # Add mean markers
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point",
               shape = 23, size = 4, 
               fill = "white", color = "gray30",
               stroke = 1.2) +
  # Apply custom colors
  scale_fill_manual(values = cyl_colors,
                    name = "Cylinders") +
  # Format y-axis
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(10, 35, by = 5),
                     limits = c(10, 35)) +
  # Add comprehensive labels
  labs(
    title = "Fuel Efficiency Decreases Dramatically with Engine Size",
    subtitle = "4-cylinder cars average 26.7 MPG compared to 15.1 MPG for 8-cylinder vehicles",
    x = "Number of Cylinders",
    y = "Miles Per Gallon (Highway)",
    caption = "Data source: 1974 Motor Trend US magazine | White diamonds indicate mean values | Visualization: Your Name"
  ) +
  # Add sample size annotations
  geom_text(data = cyl_summary,
            aes(x = cyl, y = 11, 
                label = paste0("n = ", n)),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.5, fontface = "italic", 
            color = "gray30") +
  # Add mean value annotations
  geom_text(data = cyl_summary,
            aes(x = cyl, y = 34,
                label = paste0("μ = ", round(mean_mpg, 1))),
            inherit.aes = FALSE,
            size = 3.2, fontface = "bold",
            color = "gray30") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    # Title and text styling
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 16, 
                              margin = margin(b = 8)),
    plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 11, color = "#5A6C7D", 
                                  margin = margin(b = 15)),
    plot.caption = element_text(size = 8.5, color = "#6C757D", 
                                hjust = 0, margin = margin(t = 15)),
    
    # Axis styling
    axis.title = element_text(size = 11, face = "bold", 
                              margin = margin(t = 10)),
    axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "#2C3E50"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(face = "bold", size = 11),
    
    # Legend removal
    legend.position = "none",
    
    # Grid and panel styling
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),          # Remove vertical grid
    panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#E9ECEF", linewidth = 0.5),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),            # Remove minor gridlines
    
    # Margins
    plot.margin = margin(15, 15, 15, 15)          # Add space around plot
  )

Code Explanation

Lines 2-9: Creates a summary dataframe with sample sizes, medians, and means for each cylinder group, used for annotations

Lines 12-17: Defines a custom color palette that progresses from green (efficient) to red (inefficient), optimized for colorblind accessibility

Line 19: ggplot() initializes the plot with cylinder count mapped to both x-position and fill color

Lines 21-28: geom_boxplot() creates notched box plots with custom outlier styling (hollow circles with gray borders), thicker box borders, and transparency

Lines 30-31: geom_jitter() adds individual data points with controlled horizontal spread and transparency to show the actual distribution

Lines 33-36: stat_summary() adds mean markers as white-filled diamonds, distinguishing them from the median line in the box plot

Lines 38-39: scale_fill_manual() applies our custom color palette

Lines 41-42: scale_y_continuous() sets regular y-axis breaks and limits for consistent display

Lines 44-49: labs() adds comprehensive labels including an informative title that tells the story, a subtitle with specific numbers, and detailed caption with attribution

Lines 51-57: geom_text() adds sample size annotations at the bottom of the plot area

Lines 59-64: geom_text() adds mean value annotations (using Greek letter μ) at the top of the plot area

Lines 65-93: Comprehensive theme customization including: - Enhanced typography with specific sizes, weights, and colors for hierarchy - Legend removal (since cylinder count is mapped to x-axis) - Grid customization keeping only horizontal major gridlines - Proper margins for professional spacing

Final result: A publication-ready visualization that clearly communicates the relationship between engine size and fuel efficiency. The combination of box plots (showing distribution), jittered points (showing raw data), mean markers (showing averages), and annotations (providing context) creates a comprehensive and accessible chart suitable for academic papers, reports, or presentations.

Comparison: All Three Charts

Here’s a side-by-side view of our progression:

Aspect Basic Intermediate Advanced
Readability Poor (no color, no context) Good (color-coded, points visible) Excellent (all + means + annotations)
Context None Title & labels added Full context with subtitle, caption & statistics
Visual Appeal Plain gray boxes Colored + professional theme Multi-layered + custom palette
Data Layers Box plot only Box + jittered points Box + points + mean markers
Statistical Info Quartiles only Added notches (CI) Added means, sample sizes, and outlier styling
Professional Use Not recommended Acceptable for internal use Publication-ready

Key Takeaways

Tip

Tips for Creating Better ggplot2 Box Plots:

  1. Use notches for comparisons - Notched box plots show confidence intervals around medians; non-overlapping notches suggest statistically significant differences

  2. Always show the data - For small to medium datasets (<100 points per group), overlay geom_jitter() or geom_point() to show individual observations

  3. Distinguish mean from median - Use different markers for mean (stat_summary()) and median (box plot line) when both are informative

  4. Style outliers meaningfully - Customize outlier appearance with outlier.shape, outlier.color, and outlier.size to make them visible but not distracting

  5. Color with purpose - Use color gradients or categorical colors that match the ordering or meaning of your groups

  6. Annotate sample sizes - Always show the number of observations per category so readers can assess reliability

  7. Consider orientation - Use coord_flip() for horizontal box plots when category names are long

  8. Add reference lines - Horizontal lines showing targets, thresholds, or overall means help viewers make comparisons

  9. Mind the width - Adjust box width with the width parameter (default 0.75) to control visual density

  10. Export at high resolution - Use ggsave("plot.png", width = 10, height = 6, dpi = 300) for publication-quality images

Next Steps

Try applying these principles to other comparison visualizations:

  • Violin plots for showing full distribution shapes
  • Beeswarm plots for avoiding overlap in smaller datasets
  • Ridgeline plots for comparing many groups
  • Grouped box plots using facet_wrap() for additional categorical variables

Want to create grouped box plots?

You can add a second grouping variable using position adjustments:

ggplot(data_cars, aes(x = cyl, y = mpg, fill = factor(am))) +
  geom_boxplot(position = position_dodge(width = 0.9)) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#E76F51", "#52A675"),
                    name = "Transmission",
                    labels = c("Automatic", "Manual")) +
  theme_minimal()

This creates side-by-side box plots for each combination of cylinders and transmission type.
